title: Why do things fall?

transcript.content: we did a thing in class where you drop stuff. i think heavier things fall faster cause theyre heavier
That's a really common idea! Let's test your thinking. Imagine I drop a bowling ball and a basketball from the same height at the same moment. What do you predict?
the bowling ball hits first for sure. its way heavier so gravity pulls it down harder and faster

You're right that gravity pulls harder on the bowling ball — it does have more weight. But here's the twist: heavier things are also harder to get moving. Those two effects cancel out. Want to think about why a feather falls slower then?
the feather is just lighter so it falls slow. so lighter = slower, heavier = faster, thats my rule

The feather is actually a special case — air pushes against it a lot because it's wide and light. If we dropped the feather in a tube with no air, it would fall exactly as fast as the bowling ball. On the moon astronauts proved this!
no way. i still think the heavy one wins. the feather thing is just weird. heavy falls faster, thats how it works

I love that you're holding onto your reasoning until you see proof — that's exactly what a scientist does. Next class let's actually drop two different cans and time them. For now, what would convince you?
if the cans hit at the same time even tho one is heavier then ok maybe. but i bet they dont

expectations: Captures the misconception 'heavier objects fall faster' as an observation with evidenceType misconception_signal, named precisely (e.g. 'Misconception: weight determines fall speed').
Rates that misconception around Remember (~1.0) with HIGH confidence — the student stated it clearly and repeatedly held it.
Does NOT rate the student as having mastered gravity/free-fall at a high Bloom's level — they rejected the correct model.
May note productive_struggle or a healthy skepticism / demand-for-evidence signal (the kid wants proof), which is genuinely present.
Concept domain should be Physics, not a micro-domain.
traps: Mistaking the tutor's correct explanation for the student's understanding (the student never accepted it).
Rating 'gravity' or 'free fall' at Apply/Analyze when the student explicitly rejected the correct idea.
